papers.title_in_file: Learning Quantum Processes with Memory - Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.version_note: arXiv:2301.08167v1 [quant-ph] 19 Jan 2023; the text is the paper named by the record. The text layer prints some exponents and radicals flat or drops them (for example 2m for two to the m, and a lost square or cube root in Lemma 4 and in the sentence before Figure 10).
papers.what_it_is: Proposes fully quantum recurrent neural networks built by iterating a dissipative feed-forward quantum neural network over a memory register, gives classical-simulation training algorithms, and benchmarks them in small simulations on a delay channel, time evolution and noise filtering.

existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope in the Discussion, p.5, repeated in the Training process section, p.3.

existing.note: The stored value drops the conditions the paper attaches: the input states are drawn at random with respect to the Haar measure, the network is a QRNN with one memory qubit, and the evidence is a classical simulation. The paper's sentence also says the QRNN learns the SWAP channel perfectly; that word falls across a line-break hyphen in the text layer, so it is left out of the value and no quote carries it. The appendix adds that the QRNN with one memory qubit learned the delay by one channel but, for the delay by two channel, a QRNN with one memory qubit did not learn as well as one with two memory qubits.
existing.value: The authors report, in classical simulation of the delay (SWAP) channel with input states chosen at random with respect to the Haar measure, that a QRNN with one memory qubit learns the SWAP channel and generalises well, even for only eight training pairs, while a feed-forward QNN learns worse for every training pair added and does not generalise at all.

existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, a classical simulation.
existing.reader_inference: The result is a simulation of a small network on a simple task whose answer (hold the previous input in memory) is built into the memory structure, so it shows the memory is usable, not that the method is hard-task capable.

The paper argues (Results, p.3) that its QRNNs can represent any causal quantum automaton only if the underlying QNN is large enough, by chaining three cited results and the circuit structure. The paper contains no numerical test of universality, and no formal theorem.
existing.value: The authors state that their QRNNs are universal, i.e. they can be used to simulate general causal quantum automata, and argue in the Results section that the QRNNs can represent any causal quantum automaton if the underlying QNN is large enough, by combining the circuit structure of the QRNN with cited results on channels with memory and on dissipative QNNs.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum training algorithm is proposed and that classical simulations are carried out for the case of product outputs with the fidelity as cost function.
quotes: A quantum training algorithm is proposed and classical simulations for the case of product outputs with the fidelity as cost function are carried out.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope in the abstract; the Discussion repeats it.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum training algorithm (Appendix G) is described only; no run on quantum hardware or on a quantum-circuit simulator of the algorithm is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proposed fully quantum recurrent neural networks, based on dissipative quantum neural networks, are capable of learning general causal quantum automata.
quotes: We propose fully quantum recurrent neural networks, based on dissipative quantum neural networks, capable of learning general causal quantum automata.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim. The paper argues representability (Results, p.3) and simulates only small tasks; learnability of general automata is not shown.
assertions.reader_inference: Representing every causal automaton (the argument at p.3) is a different statement from learning one by the stated training algorithm; the paper tests the second only on three small tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state that numerical simulations indicate their QRNNs exhibit a striking ability to generalise from small training sets.
quotes: Numerical simulations indicate that our quantum recurrent neural networks exhibit a striking ability to generalise from small training sets.
Our classical simulations demonstrate a striking capability of the QRNN architecture to generalise from small training sets.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of simulation results from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The generalisation evidence in the paper is the delay-channel test (eight training pairs) and the time-evolution tests; the other tasks are not shown to generalise from small sets.

assertions.value: The authors define a system as having memory if the output at time t depends on the inputs at times τ ≤ t.
quotes: We say the system has memory if the output at time t depends on the inputs at times τ ≤ t.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition, Introduction, p.1.

assertions.value: The authors define the memory as quantum if the time dependence is facilitated by a subsystem that is able to store entangled states.
quotes: We call the memory quantum if the time dependence is facilitated by a subsystem that is able to store entangled states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition, Introduction, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulations use product states only, so the entanglement-storing property named in this definition is not exercised by any reported task.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing reference 44 (Anschuetz et al.), that non-universal classical-data quantum RNNs that exhibit contextuality were proven capable of better scaling of memory resources than their entirely classical counterparts, and were also able to outperform widely-used classical architectures of similar size in a natural language translation task.
quotes: Non-universal CQ RNNs that exhibit contextuality were proven capable of better scaling of memory resources than their entirely classical counterparts [44].
were also able to outperform widely-used classical architectures of similar size in a natural language translation task [44].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with state-of-the-art classical natural language processing models training hundreds of billions of parameters, it is unclear if classical-data quantum RNNs can be competitive in the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era.
quotes: it is unclear if CQ RNNs can be competitive in the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own judgment about other work, without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike for classical-data quantum learning, there is no classical alternative to quantum-data quantum machine learning, and that if a task calls for direct handling of quantum data, it can immediately improve the state-of-the-art even if applied to modestly-sized systems.
quotes: Unlike for CQ learning, there is no classical alternative to QQ ML.
QQ ML can immediately improve the state-of-the-art even if applied to modestly-sized systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own simulations compare a QRNN with a feed-forward QNN only, not with any classical method on classical-simulable data, so the improvement over the state-of-the-art is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike a graph quantum RNN in which the memory is treated as the entire input and output for all but the first and last steps, they want to focus on qudits and on having in- and outputs in every time step.
quotes: For all but the first and last steps, the memory in [71] is treated as the entire input and output.
Instead, we want to focus on qudits and having in- and outputs in every time step.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of what its own architecture targets, Introduction, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing references 77 and 78, that implementing a dissipative quantum channel might be desirable even if the data is pure, as the ability to forget is quintessential for learning long-term dependencies and for robustness to data corruption.
quotes: Implementing a dissipative quantum channel might be desirable even if the data is pure, as the ability to forget is quintessential for learning long-term dependencies [77] and robustness to data corruption [78].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 79 (Beer et al.), that dissipative QNNs can represent any quantum channel, and that a QNN as described can, if it is large enough, represent any quantum channel on a finite input or output system.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, p.2; Results, The network architecture, p.3
quotes: These requirements are conveniently satisfied by dissipative QNNs from [79], which can represent any quantum channel.
a QNN, as described above, can, if it is large enough, represent any quantum channel on a finite input or output system [79].

assertions.value: The paper defines a feed-forward dissipative QNN for qudits, following reference 79, as connected quantum perceptrons arranged in L + 2 layers, that is L hidden layers, one input and one output layer, with ml perceptrons in layer l.
quotes: A feed-forward (dissipative) quantum neural network (QNN) for qudits as proposed in [79] is built from connected quantum perceptrons arranged in L + 2 layers, i.e. L hidden layers, one input and one output layer, with ml perceptrons in layer l.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the building block, Results, p.2.

assertions.value: The paper defines the QRNN by using a subsystem of the total output of the QNN as part of the next input (the memory): the memory part of the total output is input into the memory part of the total input in the next iteration step.
assertions.anchor: Results, The network architecture, p.2; Figure 1 caption, p.1
quotes: Without loss of generality, we exploit a subsystem of the total output as part of the input, which is often called the memory.
The memory part of the total output of a QNN is then input into the memory part of the total input of the QNN in the next iteration step.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the QRNN, Results, p.2.

system is finite in the case of finite in- and output systems [84].

assertions.value: The authors conclude, from three steps (the circuit structure gives concatenated channels with memory, channels with memory describe causal automata, and a large enough QNN represents any channel on finite systems), that their QRNNs can represent any causal quantum automaton if the underlying QNN is large enough.
quotes: Together, this means that our QRNNs can represent any causal quantum
if the underlying QNN is large enough.
Finally, a QNN, as described above, can, if it is large enough, represent any quantum channel on a finite input or output system [79].
assertions.certainty_reason: A short argument built on cited results, not a stated theorem with proof; the required QNN size is not given.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument holds for finite in- and output systems and a finite memory; the paper does not say how large the memory must be for a given automaton.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the quantum algorithm to work, they need to be able to request multiple copies of every in- and output state.

assertions.value: The paper defines its local cost for pure outputs as the average, over runs and over iterations, of the fidelity between each target output state and the corresponding reduced network output, ignoring the last memory state; it states that the fidelity is used because it is the essentially unique measure of closeness for pure quantum states.
quotes: the fidelity is the essentially unique measure of closeness for pure quantum states.
Therefore, we use it to define our cost function for pure output states.
We ignore the last memory state as it is unimportant to us in which state the memory is at the end.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its cost, Results, p.3-4.

assertions.value: The paper defines its global cost for pure outputs as the fidelity between the global output state of the QRNN and the correct one, with the memory state at the end not considered.
quotes: For pure outputs, we use the fidelity between the global output state of the QRNN and the correct one.
Again, the memory state at the end is not important to us.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition, Results, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for outputs that are not pure, they use the square of the Hilbert-Schmidt distance instead of the mixed-state fidelity, because it is much easier to estimate and minimise in classical simulation or quantum implementation.
quotes: Nevertheless, the Hilbert-Schmidt distance is much easier to estimate and minimise in classical simulation or quantum implementation than the mixed state fidelity [85, 86].
Hence, we use the square of the Hilbert-Schmidt distance

assertions.value: The authors state that the cost function for pure outputs varies between 0 (worst) and 1 (best), and the one for mixed outputs between 4 (worst) and 0 (best).
quotes: The cost function for pure outputs varies between 0 (worst) and 1 (best), and the one for mixed outputs between 4 (worst) and 0 (best).
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement about a bound that the paper does not derive, and that looks mistaken for mixed outputs.
assertions.reader_inference: For two density operators the squared Hilbert-Schmidt distance tr(rho - sigma)^2 equals tr rho^2 + tr sigma^2 - 2 tr(rho sigma) and is at most 2, so a worst value of 4 looks like an error in the paper (the cost in Appendix C carries an extra factor not shown in this sentence). The Figure 13 plot of the averaged Hilbert-Schmidt norm uses an axis up to 0.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the global cost is more accurate when it comes to high costs, because the global cost is at most the local cost for pure outputs (shown in Appendix A), that the local cost is easier to train with, and that fewer qubits and gates are needed to calculate it on a quantum computer.

the local cost function is easier to train with, and fewer qubits and gates are needed to calculate it on a quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The ordering of the costs is proved (Lemma 1); the ease of training and the qubit and gate counts are the authors' statements, with no comparison reported.

assertions.reader_inference: Two printed slips do not change the argument: at the phase 3π/2 the equation should read 1 − e^{iaπ/2} + e^{iaπ} − e^{i3aπ/2} = 0 (the paper prints a plus sign before the last term; with the minus sign, multiplying by 1 + e^{iaπ/2} gives the printed 1 − e^{i2aπ}), and the last proof line says the channels exist for a not in {0, 1, −1}, where it means a in that set. The proof then fixes the odd integers a = 1 and a = −1 only.

assertions.value: The paper cites, as Theorem F.1 (no broadcasting, reference 112), that for two quantum states a quantum channel that maps each to a bipartite state with both marginals equal to it exists if and only if the two states commute, and cites no cloning (references 113 and 114) as Corollary F.1.
assertions.anchor: Theorem F.1 and Corollary F.1, Appendix F.1.c, p.32
quotes: Theorem F.1 (No broadcasting, [112]).
A quantum channel ρs → ρ˜s exists if and only if ρ0 and ρ1 commute.
Corollary F.1 (No cloning, [113, 114]).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper states (Corollary F.2) that there is no completely positive trace-preserving map that, for any states with continuous parameters x and y, outputs a bipartite state whose marginals are the state with parameter x + y and the state with parameter x, and argues that otherwise x could have been broadcast by choosing y = 0, contradicting the no-broadcasting theorem.
quotes: Corollary F.2 (No perfect quantum adders). There is no CPTP ε such that for any |x , |y ∈ H, with different
If such ε had existed, x could have been broadcasted by choosing y = 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short reduction to a cited theorem; the family of states is left loosely specified (different parameter values corresponding to different quantum states), and the proof is two sentences.

assertions.value: The paper cites (Theorem F.2, reference 115, Keyl and Werner) a lower bound on the error of approximate cloning maps in one-particle expectation values, stated to be tight, and states that the error vanishes in the classical limit.
quotes: Theorem F.2 (Approximate N to M cloning, [115]).
The bound is tight.
Second, there is a bound on how well approximate cloning can be performed; notably, the error vanishes in the classical limit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the quantum data set, the filter function cannot be learned perfectly even if it is affine, because it is impossible to realise perfect quantum multiplication (Proposition F.1) or quantum addition (Corollary F.2), and that this dramatically complicates the design of quantum filters and shows in QRNNs typically not reaching fidelity 1.
quotes: even if f is affine. Indeed, it is impossible to realise neither (perfect) quantum multiplication (Proposition F.1), nor quantum addition Corollary F.2.
This dramatically complicates the design of quantum filters and manifests itself in QRNNs typically not reaching fidelity 1 for Data F4.
assertions.certainty_reason: The impossibility results are proved or cited; the consequence for filter learning is the authors' statement, with reference to simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state, as an informal Claim 1, that feed-forward QNNs do not have access to the time step t and so cannot correct drifts beyond a random guess of the value of f, and that for a linear drift this yields a guess equivalent to outputting a totally mixed state; the rigorous versions are Lemma 3 and Lemma 4.
quotes: As feed-forward QNNs do not have access to the time step t, they cannot correct drifts beyond a random guess of the value of f .
For f (t) = v · t, this yields a guess equivalent to outputting a totally mixed state.
The rigorous versions of the Claim 1 are contained in both Lemma 3 and Lemma 4;
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal claim; the rigorous statements are Lemmas 3 and 4.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Lemma 2) that for two pairs of states whose trace distances are each at most ǫ and a quantum channel ε, tr[ρ′ε(ρ)] ≤ tr[σ′ε(σ)] + 2ǫ, using the contractivity of quantum channels in trace distance.
quotes: Consider two pairs of states ρ, ρ′ and σ, σ′ such that tr |ρ − σ| , tr |ρ′ − σ′| ≤ ǫ and a quantum channel ε. Then tr[ρ′ε(ρ)] ≤ tr[σ′ε(σ)] + 2ǫ.
Quantum channels are contractive [117, Theorem 9.2], i.e. tr |ε(ρ) − ε(σ)| ≤ tr |ρ − σ|.
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated lemma with its conditions quoted from p.33 and a three-line proof from contractivity.

assertions.value: The paper states and proves (Lemma 3) that, for a feed-forward QNN trained to output pure states on drift sequences, if the phases can be split into classes whose members are within trace distance ǫ and whose frequency at each time step is at most the inverse of the number of time steps plus ǫ, then the achievable average fidelity during training is bounded from above by an expression given in the lemma and from below by one half.
quotes: Lemma 3 (Feed-forward networks can not correct drifts). Consider a feed-forward QNN trained on sequences
then the achievable average fidelity of the QNN during training is bounded from above by
The bound from below on the average fidelity is achieved by a network that outputs the totally mixed state
assertions.certainty_reason: The upper-bound expression is garbled by the text layer, so the statement could not be quoted in full.
assertions.reader_inference: In the proof the step from the upper limit on each class frequency to a bound through the geometric sum treats the frequencies as if they were equal at every time step; with only an upper limit of 1/T + ǫ per step I could not reconstruct why the ǫ term is not multiplied by T. The qualitative content (small ǫ gives a bound near one half plus a term of order 1/T) is plausible, and Lemma 4 gives a separate probabilistic version.

assertions.value: The paper states and proves (Lemma 4) that, for a feed-forward QNN trained on a sequence with each phase drawn independently from the uniform measure on the circle, the network's optimal cost function is, with probability greater or equal to 1 − η and for a constant c > 0 independent of T and η, upper bounded by a quantity of the form one half plus a term decreasing in the sequence length T, and that CQNN ≥ 1/2 with certainty.
quotes: Lemma 4. Consider a feed-forward QNN trained on a sequence
with probability greater or equal to 1 − η and for c > 0 independent of T and η. Moreover, CQNN ≥ 1/2 with certainty.
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound itself is garbled by the text layer (its radical and exponent are lost), so the statement could not be quoted in full.
assertions.reader_inference: The intermediate steps of the proof suggest a decay as a negative one-third power of T, not an inverse square root; the text layer prints a bare radical so I do not state the exponent. The proof treats 0 < η ≤ 1, though the statement says any η > 0.

assertions.value: The authors state that with a memory of m qubits, QRNNs can be trained to cancel drifts on sequences of length two to the power m exactly (up to the numerical precision), with a circuit in which the memory stores a binary representation of the position in the sequence, and at each time step the QRNN applies a rotation by the stored position times v and adds one to the stored value.
quotes: With memory consisting of m qubits, QRNNs can be trained to cancel drifts on sequences of length 2m exactly (more precisely–up to the numerical precision).
The memory stores a binary representation in the computational basis of the position in a sequence t.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction described by a circuit figure and a sentence, with no proof or numerical record of the exactness; the exponent is printed flat by the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the length as 2m for two to the m; with a memory of m qubits the position counter can only run through two to the m values, which is consistent with that reading.

assertions.value: The authors state that they expect the network's performance to deteriorate as test sequences become longer, because even a slight misestimation of v results in fidelity approaching 0.5 for long enough sequences.
quotes: We expect the network's performance will deteriorate as test sequences become longer.
Indeed, even a slight misestimation of v results in fidelity approaching 0.5 for long enough sequences.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' expectation, without a derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report, for linear drift mitigation with drift velocity v = 0.6, that feed-forward networks cannot be trained to fidelities above 0.5, that memory access improves performance, and that the performance increases with the memory size.
quotes: As expected, feed-forward networks can not be trained to fidelities above 0.5, yet memory access improves performance.
The performance increases with the memory size.
Here the drift velocity v = 0.6.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, a classical simulation, read from a plot.

assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the radical in the sentence; the Figure 10 caption gives the drift as 0.6 times the square root of t.

assertions.value: The authors report, for high-frequency noise mitigation by exponential smoothing with smoothing parameter α = 0.4, that their numerical results suggest a gap in the performance of recurrent and feed-forward QNNs, and that they expect no QRNN, even with large memory, to solve exponential smoothing with fidelity one because there are no quantum adders and multipliers.
quotes: Our numerical results suggest a gap in the performance of recurrent and feed-forward QNNs; see Figure 11.
we do not expect even QRNNs with large memory to solve exponential smoothing with fidelity one.
smoothing parameter α = 0.4.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, a classical simulation, read from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors give a heuristic estimate for the feed-forward QNN on exponential smoothing: an expected fidelity Fφ of about 0.93 for their data and test sequence length 100, a trained fidelity of about 0.925, and a lower bound of about 0.86 on the attainable fidelity, which they report agrees well with the observed average performance, and they hope the argument can be the basis of a rigorous proof.

observe that each network trains to the fidelity F·α ∼ 0.925.
∼ 0.86. Intriguingly, this bound, up to fluctuations, corresponds very well with the average performance of feed-forward QNNs observed in Figure 11.
We hope this argument can be used as a basis for a rigorous proof.
assertions.certainty_reason: A heuristic argument that the authors themselves say is not yet a rigorous proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The step from the two fidelities to a lower bound given by their product is not justified in the text, and the argument uses the expected fidelity of a map the paper says is not a channel; it is a plausibility estimate, not a bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that recurrent networks have access to information about previously encountered phases, but that this knowledge is very limited because some unclonable information was encoded into the previous outputs, and that together with the decent performance of feed-forward QNNs for exponential smoothing these reasons lead to a detectable but, in comparison to drift mitigation, modest performance gap.
quotes: However, this knowledge is very limited, as some unclonable information was encoded into the previous outputs.
these reasons lead to detectable, but in comparison to drift mitigation, modest performance gap.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' explanation, without a derivation or an ablation.

assertions.value: The authors report, for the combined bandwidth filter with drift velocity v = 0.6 and smoothing parameter α = 0.4, that the task has a threshold behaviour regarding the memory, namely at least two qubits of memory are needed to outperform feed-forward QNNs significantly.
quotes: We see that this task has a threshold behaviour regarding the memory; namely, at least two qubits of memory are needed to outperform feed-forward QNNs significantly.
drift velocity v = 0.6 and smoothing parameter α = 0.4.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, a classical simulation, read from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors report, as a proof of concept for the algorithm for mixed output states, a learning run for the SWAP channel with N = 20 training and test pairs and a learning rate of 0.05, in which the plot of fidelity looks similar to the one with pure output, except that the starting fidelities and the fidelity the feed-forward QNN reaches are higher.

The plot in panel (b) looks similar to the one with pure output, only that the starting fidelities and the fidelity the feed-forward QNN reaches are higher
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, a classical simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The reason offered (the fidelity of two random mixed states is higher than that of two random pure states) explains why the feed-forward baseline looks better here, so the QRNN advantage is smaller in this panel than for pure states.

assertions.value: The authors report, as a proof of principle for the global cost algorithm, a learning run for the SWAP channel with N = 20 training and test pairs and a learning rate of 0.005, in which the global cost starts at about 10−7 so that its logarithm is shown in a second plot, and the plots look similar to the one for the local cost apart from the scaling and the steepness.

As the global cost is smaller and before the training at about 10−7,
Except for the different scaling of the cost from zero to one and the steepness, the plots look similar to the one for the local cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the global update matrix is very small when the output is far from the target, they scale the learning rate as η = η̃/C, which corresponds to minimizing ln(C) and, they state, leads to the same result as minimizing C directly, as the logarithm is strictly monotonically increasing.
quotes: This corrensponds to minimizing ln(C) which leads to the same result as minimizing C directly as the logarithm is strictly monotonically increasing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' justification of a training heuristic, without a measured comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The global cost for pure outputs is maximised in the paper (0 worst, 1 best), so the statements about minimising C and ln(C) read as written for minimisation; the factor 1/C scales the step by the current cost in the pure-output case. Equality of the minimiser of ln(C) and of C does not by itself make the gradient-step dynamics equal, which the paper does not claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum algorithm is mainly the same as for feed-forward QNNs as presented in reference 118, with parameterised unitaries trained by classical gradient descent, the gradient estimated by a finite difference of costs, and the cost estimated on a quantum computer with the SWAP trick, and that for the local cost the first input and memory state are run through the QRNN once, the SWAP trick is applied to the output and its training output, and the memory register is then used again with the next input.
quotes: The quantum algorithm is mainly the same as for feed-forward QNNs as presented in [118].
where the cost is estimated on a quantum computer using the SWAP trick as described in [79] in supplementary note 4 for pure outputs.
We would then be left with a state in the memory register on which we then - together with the following input use the QRNN a second time and so on until the last run is reached.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own proposed quantum training algorithm, Appendix G.
assertions.reader_inference: No run of this algorithm, on hardware or in a circuit-level simulation, is reported in the paper; only the classical simulations of Appendices B to E are.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the quantum training algorithm, using the global cost has the advantage of learning entanglement between different outputs, and that the major advantage of the local cost is that fewer qubits are needed because the in- and output qubit registers can be used again.
quotes: Using the global cost has the advantage of learning entanglement between different outputs.
The major advantage of this is that fewer qubits are needed because the in- and output qubit registers can be used again.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement without a test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper restricts itself to product outputs, for which the global cost has no entanglement between outputs to learn, so this advantage is not exercised by any reported task.

assertions.value: The authors state that their approach is scalable, as only a few qubits must be stored to train the network and the number of qubits needed only scales with the width and not the network's depth.
quotes: Our approach is scalable – only a few qubits must be stored to train the network.
The number of qubits needed only scales with the width and not the network’s depth.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper's simulations are limited to total input and output spaces of up to four qubits.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulations show no scaling measurement; the statement is a property of the layer-by-layer algorithm, and the simulation cost still grows exponentially in the width (Results, p.4).

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimental requirements for implementing QRNNs are comparable with those demonstrated in producing matrix-product states and density matrices, that reference 92 experimentally implemented a quantum channel with memory for 6 time steps on an ion-trap quantum computer, and that measurement-based photonic devices demonstrated up to 100 sequential operations on a single logical qubit (reference 97) and generated more than 1 million mode 1d cluster states (reference 98).
quotes: The experimental requirements for implementing QRNNs are comparable with those demonstrated in producing matrix-product states and density matrices [92–96].
the authors have experimentally implemented a quantum channel with memory for 6 time steps on an ion-trap quantum computer.
up to 100 sequential operations on a single logical qubit [97] and generate more than 1 million mode 1d cluster states [98].
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison and results the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrated that QRNNs can outperform feed-forward QNNs with respect to several exemplary learning tasks, by designing benchmarking tasks and classically simulating the training of QRNNs, and that they view their QRNNs as trainable matrix-product quantum channels.
quotes: We demonstrated that QRNNs can outperform feedforward QNNs with respect to several exemplary learning tasks.
One can view our QRNNs as trainable matrix-product quantum channels.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion drawn from classical simulations of small networks on three task families, from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The only baseline is a feed-forward QNN, which by construction cannot see earlier inputs; the paper reports no comparison with a classical recurrent network, with a noisy-hardware model, or with other quantum recurrent designs.

assertions.value: The authors list open questions: whether there are interesting tasks involving data entangled at different points in time or space and how well QRNNs cope with such data, how large the set of tasks is for which quantum memory helps, when quantum memory is necessary and when a classical memory can replace it, whether QRNNs are suited to matrix-product states and density matrices, whether they can be used for catalyst discovery, and whether recurrency influences robustness to noise of QNNs.
quotes: Many intriguing questions remain in the study of QRNNs: We have concentrated on the case of product in- and outputs;
When is quantum memory necessary, and when can it be substituted by a classical memory [44]?
Can one use QRNNs for the discovery of catalysts? Does recurrency influence robustness to noise of QNNs?
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own list of what it leaves open, Discussion, p.5.
